title: 'Abasa: look at your food
hookLine: let the human look at his food: rain, grain, grapes, olives, palms (80:24–32)
tomorrow: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother
last: 'ABASA — TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.

cards: Where did your last meal come from? The quick answer is usually a store, a delivery bag, a drive-through window. Maybe a plastic tray with a sticker on it.
The food shows up already finished, with the whole story cut off. Somewhere there was rain, and dirt, and a seed, and months of sun, and people bent over in a field.
None of that is on the sticker. 'Abasa, after the story of the frown, turns to a very different subject, and asks for a slower kind of looking.

teach.b: Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's words: Let man consider his food. Look at it. Then the surah tells the story behind the plate, starting in the sky.
We pour water down in showers. Then We split the earth open, in clefts.
Then We cause grain to grow in it, and grapes, and green fodder, and olive trees and date palms, and gardens thick with trees, and fruit, and grasses. Provision for you, and for your animals.

Rain, cracked soil, a sprout, a harvest, like a slow-motion film of a seed. The whole cycle is a gift, set down in front of you. One word in that list is well-known for a different reason: abb, grasses.
A report in the commentaries says that 'Umar, one of the closest companions, read this verse, admitted he didn't know exactly what abb meant, and decided not to force a meaning onto it.
Commentators explain it as pasture, the plants that animals graze.
But the honesty is worth keeping: even 'Umar could say, I don't know exactly.
Notice where the passage sits: right after the surah reminds the human being he was made from a drop, and asks why he is ungrateful. The answer to ingratitude isn't a lecture.
It's: look at your plate. Trace one bite back to the rain. Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after: two small words to bracket the story.

how: Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, eat with the right hand, and try not to waste food; these verses of 'Abasa are recalled as a reminder that a meal begins with rain.

games.q: the story of your food, backward — tap the pairs.

s: every word in 'Abasa was perfectly clear to the first Muslims
a report in the commentaries says 'Umar admitted he didn't know exactly what abb meant.
the passage traces food back to rain
water poured down, earth split open, then grain, grapes, olives and palms.
the surah says the provision is for people only
it says for you and for your cattle.

games.q: 'Umar reads the word abb and isn't sure what it means. what does he do, according to the report?
o: admits he doesn't know and doesn't force one
games.why: he admits it and lets it be. in the report, honesty about not knowing comes before guessing.

practice: Choose one thing you ate today or will eat soon, a piece of bread, an apple, rice. Trace it backward: the kitchen, the store, the truck, the field, the hands that picked it, the sun, the rain, the seed.
When you reach the rain, stop, and just hold it.

wordCard.voice: 'Abasa. He frowned, Surah eighty, which also says: let the human look at his food, rain to grain to fruit. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "his food," from ta'am, food, what is tasted (Qur'an 80:24).

carryVoice: Your line: look at your food. Every meal begins with rain. Day two hundred fourteen, done.
